title: The Rise and Fall of Quibi: How $1.75 Billion Vanished in Six Months
creator: Noor Haddad
description:
Quibi had Hollywood's biggest names, a billion-dollar war chest and a launch party money can't buy. Six months later it was gone. Here's what happened.

Sources: press coverage from 2019 to 2020, the founders' own interviews, and app store data. Full list in the pinned comment.

This channel is supported by viewers. Thank you.

sentences.t: In April of twenty twenty, an app launched with more money behind it than almost any startup in history.
By December it was dead.
This is the story of Quibi.
So, quick background.
Quibi was the idea of Jeffrey Katzenberg, the guy who ran Disney's film studio in its nineties golden age and then co-founded DreamWorks.
He teamed up with Meg Whitman, the former boss of eBay and Hewlett Packard.
And their pitch was simple.
People watch video on their phones, in little gaps of their day, so let's make Hollywood quality shows, but in chapters of ten minutes or less.
Quick bites, that's literally where the name comes from.
And investors loved it.
Quibi raised around one point seven five billion dollars before it launched a single show, from basically every major studio in Hollywood.
Quibi signed deals with huge names, directors, movie stars, people who would never normally make something for a phone.
Quibi even had a feature called Turnstyle, where a show would switch from horizontal to vertical as you rotated your phone, and they were very proud of it.
The launch plan was a ninety-day free trial, and then Quibi would cost about five dollars a month with ads, or eight without.
And Quibi spent a fortune on marketing, including a Super Bowl spot, before most people even knew what the app was.
So what went wrong?
Well, the obvious answer is timing.
Quibi launched in April of twenty twenty, right as the whole world went into lockdown.
And the entire product was built for commuters, people on a train or waiting in line for coffee.
Suddenly nobody was commuting.
Everyone was at home, with a big TV right in front of them.
But honestly, I don't think the pandemic is the whole story.
Here's the thing that gets me.
You couldn't share clips.
In twenty twenty, an app for short videos on your phone didn't let you screenshot or share anything to social media.
So nothing went viral, because nothing could.
Meanwhile a free app full of short videos made by teenagers in their bedrooms was exploding at exactly the same time.
And then there's the content itself.
A lot of the shows were fine.
Some were even good.
But nobody could tell you what Quibi was for, or why you'd pay for it instead of everything else you already paid for.
After the free trial ended, most people just didn't convert.
By October, the founders wrote an open letter saying they were shutting down.
They said the idea wasn't strong enough to justify a standalone service, or that the timing was wrong, and they couldn't tell which.
And I actually respect that honesty a little bit.
They gave a lot of the money back to investors instead of burning all of it.
The content library was later sold to another streaming company for a tiny fraction of what it cost.
So what's the lesson?
I think it's that money can't buy you a reason to exist.
You can hire every star in Hollywood, but if the product fights how people actually behave, they'll just go somewhere else.
Next time I'm looking at another huge flop from the same year, so subscribe if you don't want to miss it.
